# Retrospective {#sec-retrospective} **You will learn:** - what the rank sweep asks, what it changes and what it holds fixed; - what the adapter of @sec-training can and cannot say about the rank it needs; - how many trainable parameters an adapter of each rank adds; - what is written down before the results of the sweep are seen. The book fine-tuned one model, with one adapter, and a few choices were made without testing the alternatives. This chapter runs one experiment on one of them: a **rank sweep**, the same fine-tuning run at five values of the LoRA rank (@sec-lora), compared on the same validation turns. Afterwards it goes through the other things one could try, and says for each what the earlier chapters already show. ## The experiment The sweep trains four new adapters, with ranks 4, 8, 32 and 64, and sets them beside the rank-16 adapter of @sec-training. The rank is the only thing that changes (with `alpha`, which moves with it so that the scaling stays the same). The data, the learning rate, the number of epochs, the batch size and the seed are those of @sec-training. The sweep asks three things: 1. Does a smaller rank do as well as 16? 2. Does a larger rank do better? 3. Does an adapter with more directions use them? The first two are answered by the accuracy of each adapter on the validation split, in both history modes (@sec-evaluating), and by its paired difference from the rank-16 adapter. The third is answered by the same analysis of the adapter's update that @sec-training made for rank 16. The training loss of each run is the check that the runs differ only in capacity, and not in how they trained. The rest of the chapter sets the sweep up. The next sections say why the rank is the thing to vary and what the rank-16 adapter already tells us, then define the runs and the size of each adapter, and then write down what we expect and how we will read the results, before any of them is seen. ## Why the rank ::: {#9e597822 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} from peft import LoraConfig default_rank = LoraConfig().r assert default_rank != 16 ``` ::: The adapter of @sec-training has rank $r = 16$: each adapted matrix is changed by the product of two thin matrices with 16 directions between them. The rank is the capacity of the update. A task that needs the model to change a lot needs a high rank; one that asks for a small, regular change, such as writing programs in a fixed format, may need very little. We fixed 16 before looking at the task, and nothing in the book has tested it. It is not even the default of the PEFT library, which is 8. Full fine-tuning, where every direction of every matrix may change, is not run: the highest rank of the sweep is the nearest it gets. ## What the first adapter says @sec-training looked at the update that the rank-16 adapter made, one matrix at a time, and found that it was small compared with the weights and that it was concentrated in a few directions. ::: {#5be3046d .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from convfinqa.artifacts import get stats = get("adapter_analysis_main_0").json("stats.json") sq = np.array([m["singular_values"] for m in stats["matrices"]]) ** 2 share = sq / sq.sum(1, keepdims=True) cumulative = share.cumsum(1).mean(0) assert stats["r"] == 16 assert share[:, 0].mean() > 0.4 and cumulative[7] > 0.85 ``` ::: The largest direction holds on average 56% of the squared norm of an update, and the largest eight hold 93%. That suggests that a rank below 16 might do. It cannot say more than that. An update made with 16 directions is cut off at 16: if the task could use 64, the rank-16 adapter would show a spread that runs to the last direction, and would not show the directions it did not have. The sweep is the way to find out, and the same analysis of a larger adapter says whether it uses the extra directions. ## The runs The ranks are 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64, with 16 in the middle. The rank-16 run is the adapter that every earlier chapter used (`main`). Each of the others is the same run with the rank changed and `alpha` set to twice the rank, so that the scaling $\alpha / r$ that multiplies the update stays at 2 (@sec-lora). They are defined in `configs/train.json` as `rank4`, `rank8`, `rank32` and `rank64`, and each gives the artifacts of @sec-training and @sec-evaluating with its name in place of `main`: `lora_rank64_0` is the adapter, `tuned_val_rank64_0_pred` its answers on the validation split. The seed is 0 for all of them. The number of parameters of an adapter grows in proportion to the rank. For each adapted matrix of shape $d_\text{out} \times d_\text{in}$ the adapter has $r (d_\text{in} + d_\text{out})$ parameters, and the model adapts every linear layer of each of its blocks. ::: {#d83f4137 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} from transformers import AutoConfig MODEL = "Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507" cfg = AutoConfig.from_pretrained(MODEL) d, heads, kv, hd = ( cfg.hidden_size, cfg.num_attention_heads, cfg.num_key_value_heads, cfg.head_dim, ) # (input size, output size) of the seven adapted matrices of a block SHAPES = { "q_proj": (d, heads * hd), "k_proj": (d, kv * hd), "v_proj": (d, kv * hd), "o_proj": (heads * hd, d), "gate_proj": (d, cfg.intermediate_size), "up_proj": (d, cfg.intermediate_size), "down_proj": (cfg.intermediate_size, d), } per_rank = cfg.num_hidden_layers * sum(i + o for i, o in SHAPES.values()) # the adapter that was trained has the size the formula gives from safetensors import safe_open with safe_open( get("lora_main_0").path / "adapter" / "adapter_model.safetensors", "pt" ) as f: trained = sum( np.prod(f.get_slice(k).get_shape()) for k in f.keys() ) assert trained == 16 * per_rank RANKS = [4, 8, 16, 32, 64] pd.DataFrame({ "rank": RANKS, "alpha": [2 * r for r in RANKS], "trainable parameters": [f"{r * per_rank:,}" for r in RANKS], }).set_index("rank") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
alpha trainable parameters
rank
4 8 8,257,536
8 16 16,515,072
16 32 33,030,144
32 64 66,060,288
64 128 132,120,576
``` ::: ::: The adapter of rank 16 has 33\,030\,144 parameters, which is what the adapter file of `main` holds; each step in the table doubles it, and at rank 64 it has 132 million. ## What is decided before the results One seed per rank is what the budget allows, and that limits what the results can say. The comparison of each run with `main` is a paired difference on the same validation turns (@sec-evaluating). When its interval excludes zero, that run differs from `main` on this split. It does not say the rank is the cause: two runs of the same rank with different seeds also differ, by an amount the sweep does not measure. So a small difference, in either direction, will be reported as not shown, and the sweep is read as a curve: whether the accuracy rises, falls or is flat as the rank changes, not whether any one point is better. The prediction, written before any of these runs: the accuracy is flat from rank 4 to rank 64, with differences that the paired intervals cannot tell from zero. The reasons are that the update at rank 16 is already concentrated in few directions (see "What the first adapter says" above) and that the format of the task is simple. The prediction would fail if the accuracy rose with the rank beyond 16, or fell sharply at the low end (at rank 4 or 8, because the capacity is too small). Rank 64 is four times the default, and the evidence above gives no reason to expect the task to use more. The sweep stops there unless the accuracy is still rising at rank 64, that is, unless rank 64 differs from `main` by a paired interval that excludes zero. In that case ranks 128 and 256 are the next runs, and this chapter will say so.
